To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

binaural sensitivity is determined by the binaural critical band, that binaural detection is based on the detection of a binaural envelope correlation, and that binaural envelope correlations are computed from the monaural envelopes by means of a cross-correlation.
the model predicts the binaural detection threshold for a given masker and signal as a function of masker and signal frequency, bandwidth, and interaural phase relation.

the binaural detection threshold is a function of the binaural critical band of the masker (the bandwidth of the filter with the highest response to the masker) and of the masker level, and that this binaural critical-band concept is independent of the interaural time difference of the masker.

the question of how a binaural auditory signal-processing system may work, which spectral parameters are relevant, and how they are processed.
the development of a computational model for binaural signal processing.

the development of a computational model that can be used as a tool for studying the signal-processing capabilities of the binaural system and for predicting its performance in various listening conditions.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the binaural system can be modeled as a combination of a monaural preprocessing stage and an optimal binaural detector, with the latter stage accounting for the binaural enhancement of signal-to-noise ratios.
the model can account for a large set of experimental data on binaural detection, discrimination, and masking.

a model of the signal processing in binaural hearing can be developed based on the known physiological mechanisms and that this model can predict the effects of the spectral parameters on binaural detection and discrimination thresholds.
